learn.title: A shorthand for growth
learn.body: Counting steps gives exact formulas like $3n + 5$. For large n only the biggest term matters, and constant factors depend on the machine. Big O keeps just the shape of the growth. We write $3n + 5$ as $O(n)$, said big O of n.

learn.title: Two rules
learn.body: Rule 1: drop constant factors, so $3n$ becomes $n$. Rule 2: keep only the fastest growing term, so $n^2 + n$ becomes $n^2$. Big O is an upper bound: it says the work grows no faster than this shape.

learn.title: Three loops, three shapes
learn.body: The first line is one step. The loop is about n steps. The nested loops are about n times n.

learn.title: Combine the parts
learn.body: The code above takes about $1 + n + n^2$ steps.
steps: What is left is $n^2$, so the code is $O(n^2)$

learn.title: Common growth rates
learn.body: From slowest growing to fastest: $O(1)$ constant, $O(\log n)$ logarithmic, $O(n)$ linear, $O(n \log n)$, $O(n^2)$ quadratic. Reading `a[0]` is $O(1)$. A single loop is $O(n)$. Two nested loops are $O(n^2)$. Halving the input again and again is $O(\log n)$.
Big O ignores small inputs. An $O(n)$ code can be slower than an $O(n^2)$ code for tiny n, but as n grows the shape always wins.

questions.explanation: Drop the constant factor 3 and the lower term 5, leaving $n$.

questions.prompt: What is $n^2 + n$ in big O?
questions.explanation: $n^2$ grows faster than $n$, so it is the only term that matters for large n.

questions.prompt: Reading one item with `a[0]` takes \_\_ time.
questions.explanation: Reading by index takes the same single step however long the array is.
A logarithm grows very slowly. $\log n$ is smaller than $n$, which is smaller than $n^2$.

questions.prompt: Put the order from slowest growing to fastest growing.
questions.explanation: Constant is flattest, then logarithmic, linear and quadratic.

questions.prompt: Code takes $4n^2 + 10n + 7$ steps. Its big O is $O(n^k)$. What is k?
questions.explanation: The $n^2$ term dominates. After dropping 4, 10n and 7 you get $O(n^2)$.
